note_on_method: Nobody working on this has played on these courts. Portland is unusual in this directory in that almost everything below comes from a single page — Portland Parks & Recreation's own pickleball page — which is unusually forthcoming: it states a court count, a full postal address, indoor or outdoor, a surface word, a cost and whether you need to bring a net, for every venue it lists. That page is also the limit of what we know. Where it is silent, so is this page, and the silences are named rather than filled.

slots.parking: Nothing. Portland Parks & Recreation lists an address, a court count, a cost and an amenities line for each of these eleven venues, and never once mentions parking — not a lot, not a fee, not a permit, not a warning about a busy weekend. That is a real gap for six of these sites, because Columbia, Sellwood, Laurelhurst and Gabriel are large, popular parks whose car parks serve a pool, a playground or a sports field long before they serve a pickleball court. Portland also has residential permit-parking districts, and whether any of these parks falls inside one is not something the parks department says. We would rather tell you it is unverified than guess at it from a map. If you are driving to any of these for the first time, budget time to find a space and expect to walk.
slots.peak_hours: Unstated, but the city's own rules imply the shape of it. The outdoor courts are first-come, first-served, and Portland asks players to "limit play to 60 minutes when courts are in demand as a courtesy to other players" and repeats the one-hour cap in its posted rules. A city does not write a rotation rule for courts that are empty. It also says single players may not hold a court while their partner arrives, which is the kind of rule you only write after watching people do it. Beyond that, the department publishes no hours-by-hours guidance and no counts of how busy any site gets, so we have none to give. Play is dawn to dusk at every outdoor site, which in Portland means something very different in June than in December.
slots.surface_condition: This is the one place where Portland tells us something and we still decline to publish most of it. The department says "hard courts" at nine of the eleven venues, and we do not record that as a surface: asphalt, concrete and acrylic are all hard, so the word sorts courts into a category without naming a material, and our surface vocabulary refuses it for that reason. Two venues survive the test. Pier Park says "concrete", which is a material. Southwest and St. Johns community centres say "wood", which is a gym floor. Nothing at all is published about condition — no resurfacing dates, no crack reports, no comparison between sites. The one condition note the city does make is a safety one that applies everywhere: the surface is slippery when wet, which in this city is not a small caveat. Nine of eleven venues are described as having permanent lines, so you are unlikely to arrive and find nothing marked.
slots.local_scene: Portland has done something few American cities have: written down where pickleball may and may not be striped, and why. The department says most of its tennis court areas "are not far enough away from homes to properly reduce the noise from pickleball play", and that it adds pickleball striping only where there is adequate distance — which it puts at 300 to 600 feet. It names four parks as sanctioned pickleball sites: Columbia, Pier, Sellwood and Gabriel. It also concedes that some existing striping was done before the noise concerns were understood and before that distance rule existed. That is a candid piece of writing from a parks department, and it explains the map better than any court count does — this is a city where the constraint on new outdoor courts is the neighbours, not the budget. Alongside it runs an indoor programme: four community centres take drop-in players at $6 for adults and $5 for seniors, and registered play at the Portland Tennis Center and two of the centres goes through an ActiveNet account. Painting, taping or chalking your own lines on a Portland tennis court is explicitly against the rules.

best_for.heading: Best if you want the most courts in one place
best_for.text: Portland Tennis Center, with sixteen — more than any other venue in this directory. The catch is in the same sentence that gives the number: pickleball there runs as a registered summer programme, "available from mid June until early September", through an ActiveNet account, with no court reservations. Outside that window the sixteen courts are not a pickleball answer. If you want eight courts on an ordinary day in November, Columbia Park and Sellwood Park each have eight, free, and open dawn to dusk.

best_for.heading: Best if you want a court that is only ever a pickleball court
best_for.text: Gabriel Park has six courts the city describes as 'pickleball only', with permanent lines and nets included — so you can turn up carrying a paddle and nothing else. Laurelhurst Park has two on the same terms and Hillside Park has one, but Gabriel is the largest of the three and one of the four sites Portland names as sanctioned pickleball parks. Everywhere else in this city, bring your own net.

best_for.heading: Best if it is raining, which is most of the year
best_for.text: Southwest Community Center has five indoor courts on a wood floor, the most of the four centres that take drop-in players, at $6 for adults and $5 for seniors. East Portland Community Center has four, Montavilla three and St. Johns two. This is the part of Portland's provision that matters between October and May, and it is the reason the city's indoor list is worth its own page here — the free outdoor courts are dawn-to-dusk in a city where dusk arrives at half past four in December.

best_for.heading: Best if you do not want to pay anything
best_for.text: Twenty-nine outdoor courts across six parks are described by the city with one word: free. Columbia Park and Sellwood Park have eight each, Gabriel six, Pier four, Laurelhurst two and Hillside one. Portland is the first city in this directory where we can say a venue is free rather than saying we have not checked — five cities came before it and not one of their operators put a price, or the absence of one, in writing.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts does Portland have?
faqs.a: We have verified 59 across eleven venues run by Portland Parks & Recreation: 45 outdoor and 14 indoor. Six outdoor parks hold 29 of them and are free; four community centres hold 14 indoor courts at a drop-in fee; and the Portland Tennis Center accounts for 16 outdoor courts through a summer programme. That is what one city page states. It is not a claim about every court in Portland — private clubs, schools and any court the parks department does not list are outside it.

All six outdoor parks: Columbia, Pier, Sellwood, Laurelhurst, Gabriel and Hillside. The city uses the word "free" for each of them, alongside the court count, which is why we publish it as a verified fact rather than an assumption. The four community centres charge $6 for adults and $5 for seniors per drop-in session. The Portland Tennis Center states no price at all — its pickleball runs through ActiveNet registration and the page names no figure, so we have not printed one.

faqs.q: Do I need to bring my own net?
faqs.a: At most places, yes. Columbia, Pier and Sellwood all say "bring your own net" — that is 20 of the city's free courts. Nets are included at Laurelhurst and Gabriel, the two 'pickleball only' sites that say so, and provided at the Portland Tennis Center. Hillside says bring your own. For the four community centres the city does not say either way for drop-in play, so we have not answered it: two of them mention nets, but only in the description of their registered programmes, which is a different thing from what is out for a drop-in session.

faqs.q: Why does Portland have so few outdoor pickleball courts for its size?
faqs.a: Noise, and the city says so itself. Portland Parks & Recreation states that most of its tennis court areas "are not far enough away from homes to properly reduce the noise from pickleball play", and that it stripes for pickleball only where courts are roughly 300 to 600 feet from housing. It names four sanctioned pickleball parks — Columbia, Pier, Sellwood and Gabriel — and acknowledges that some earlier striping predates the rule. Very few parks departments publish their constraint this plainly.

faqs.q: Can I paint or tape my own pickleball lines on a Portland tennis court?
faqs.a: No. The department's rules say pickleball play is only permitted on pickleball courts, and that no painting, taping or chalking of lines is allowed on its tennis courts. Nine of the eleven venues verified here are described as having permanent lines already.

faqs.q: What are the courts like in winter?
faqs.a: The outdoor courts are open dawn to dusk year-round, which in Portland means a playable window of a few hours in midwinter, on surfaces the city warns are slippery when wet. That is what makes the fourteen indoor courts across the four community centres the practical answer for much of the year. What we cannot tell you is how those indoor courts are scheduled — the city points drop-in players at each community centre's own page for the timetable, and those pages are not part of what we have verified here.

faqs.q: What do you not know about these venues?
faqs.a: Three things, all of them because the city does not publish them. Lighting: not one of the eleven venues says whether its courts are lit, so every one of them reads "not verified yet" rather than "no". Parking: never mentioned, at any of them. And surface at nine of the eleven, because the city says "hard courts", which names a category rather than a material and is refused by our surface vocabulary. Pier Park's concrete and the two wood community-centre floors are the exceptions.

sources.evidence: The department's pickleball page. Court counts and addresses per venue, e.g. "Columbia Park | 4503 N Lombard St., Portland, OR 97203 / 8 Outdoor hard courts, free, permanent lines, bring your own net. Amenities: restrooms and water." Indoor drop-in pricing: "$6 for adults/$5 for seniors". Noise policy: "Most tennis court areas in our parks are not far enough away from homes to properly reduce the noise from pickleball play" and "at least 300 to 600 feet away from homes"; sanctioned parks named as "Columbia, Pier, Sellwood, and Gabriel Park". Rules: "Limit play to one hour if others are waiting", "No painting, taping, or chalking lines is allowed on PP&R tennis courts", "Be aware surface is slippery when wet", "Courts are open from Dawn to Dusk."
